lines: Morgan Patel
+1 (555) 010-4410 | morgan.patel@example.com | example.com/code/mpatel
EDUCATION
Ridgeway University | Ph.D. candidate in Statistics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2021 - Expected May 2026
Ridgeway University | B.S. in Mathematics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2016 - May 2020
EXPERIENCE
Sunrise Bakery | Assistant Store Manager | Metro City, USA | Sep 2025 - Present
- Managed opening shifts and a team of 6 bakers and cashiers, keeping the store within its weekly labour budget.
- Ran daily stock counts and supplier orders, cutting unsold bread from 12% to 7% of production.
Northpeak Capital | Quantitative Research Intern | Metro City, USA | Jun 2025 - Aug 2025
- Built a short-horizon order-book imbalance signal for liquid index futures that raised the desk book's Sharpe ratio from 1.1 to 1.5 over 18 months of out-of-sample backtest after costs.
- Cut the signal's daily turnover from 34% to 21% with a cost-aware position smoother, keeping 90% of gross returns and lowering estimated slippage by a third.
- Confirmed the forecast gain over the nested HAR-RV baseline with standard Diebold-Mariano tests across the 30 indices.
- Joining 120 microstructure features point-in-time across six venues, deduplicating late prints and versioning each schema, built a feature store the team reused in two later projects.
- Annualized the signal's daily Sharpe ratio by multiplying it by 252 before reporting it to the desk.
- Documented the backtest assumptions, transaction-cost model and known failure regimes in the desk's research wiki, which the next intern cohort used to onboard in their first week.
Ridgeway University | Research Assistant, Statistical Learning Lab | Metro City, USA | Jun 2020 - Aug 2021
- Built the lab's simulation pipeline on the shared cluster, cutting a 2,000-run Monte Carlo study from 3 days to 5 hours, with every run reproducible from its seed and configuration file.
- Derived a variance bound for a sparse regression estimator; my proof tightens the previous bound by a log factor and is now Section 3 of a paper under review at JASA.
- Taught weekly recitations for 60 students in graduate probability, writing 12 problem sets and earning a 4.8/5 teaching rating.

- Released an open-source R package for high-dimensional covariance estimation while maintaining the lab's shared cluster, organizing the weekly reading group and grading for two courses, which was downloaded 3,000 times in its first year.
PROJECTS
Volatility Forecasting Study | Independent Research | Python, PyTorch | Jan 2024 - Present
- Beat a HAR-RV baseline's out-of-sample QLIKE loss by 7% on 30 equity indices with a temporal convolutional model trained on realized-volatility features.
- Cut forecast error from 0.20 to 0.15, a 33% improvement, by adding realized-volatility features and an asymmetric loss.
- Improved the model's directional hit rate by 6% on 30 equity indices, from 52% to 58%, with a temporal convolutional model.
Kaggle Market Prediction Competition | Team of 3 | Python | Mar 2023 - Jun 2023
- Placed 41st of 2,900 teams with a gradient-boosting ensemble on 300 engineered features, finishing in the top 2% of the private leaderboard.
- Cut validation leakage by switching to time-grouped folds, which closed a 0.02 gap between local validation and leaderboard scores.
- Wrote the team's feature-selection script using permutation importance, trimming 900 candidate features to 300 without losing validation score.
SKILLS
Programming: Python, R, PyTorch, Kafka
Methods: time-series econometircs, high-dimensional statistics, gradient boosting

items.says: There is no summary or tagline to frame the quant profile immediately.
items.because: A recruiter may wonder whether the bakery role is the main current occupation.

items.says: The JASA paper is difficult to find without a separate publications section.
items.because: It is a meaningful credential whose status and authorship should be easy to assess.

items.says: The résumé does not establish live, paper-traded, or deployed strategy experience.
items.because: Some quant roles may require it, and backtests should not sound like realized performance.

items.says: Portfolio-construction and risk-control details are missing.
items.because: Sharpe and turnover claims provide only partial evidence in those areas.

items.says: Common implementation tools such as SQL and C++ are not shown.
items.because: Their absence could matter if a target posting requires them.

items.says: The skills section does not clearly distinguish tools, methods, and domain areas.
items.because: Separating them would make it easier to scan.

items.says: The code link should lead directly to a relevant, polished project or portfolio.
items.because: A general profile would be less useful.

items.says: The Ph.D. entry does not state a research focus or dissertation area.
items.because: The degree title alone does not show the candidate's specialization.

items.says: The bakery role has too much prominence for a quant application.
items.because: It leads the experience section and can obscure the candidate's current career direction.

items.says: The weekly labour-budget claim gives no scale or outcome beyond meeting budget.
items.because: Its value is hard to judge in a quant résumé.

items.says: The spelling of “labour” should be standardized for the target region.
“Unsold bread” needs a definition and measurement period.
items.because: Without them, the reduction from 12% to 7% is hard to assess.

items.says: The Sharpe figures and the meaning of “the desk book's Sharpe” need clarification.
items.because: A reader may question whether the intern-built signal caused the full change.

items.says: The signal's out-of-sample design and execution assumptions need more detail.
items.because: A quant reviewer will want to assess whether the backtest is robust and net of costs.

items.says: The basis for “90% of gross returns” is unclear.
items.because: The reader needs to know what the retained-return figure measures.

items.says: The slippage reduction needs its estimation method and estimated-versus-realized status made clear.
items.because: A backtest estimate could otherwise be mistaken for a live effect.

items.says: The turnover and performance comparisons need consistent periods and assumptions.
items.because: Otherwise their figures may not be comparable.

items.says: The Diebold–Mariano comparison does not state its forecast metric.
items.because: A technical reader needs to know what was tested.

items.says: The bullet does not establish significance or explain testing across 30 indices.
items.because: Without that scope, “confirmed” may sound stronger than the evidence supports.

items.says: The opening gerund makes the feature-store sentence awkward.
items.because: It obscures the relationship between the data-joining work and the main action.

items.says: Individual ownership of the feature store is unclear.
items.because: The reader should be able to identify the candidate's contribution.

items.says: “Reused in two later projects” needs a practical explanation.
items.because: The extent of reuse is unclear.

items.says: Multiplying daily Sharpe by 252 is the wrong standard annualization calculation.
items.because: Under the usual independent-return assumption, the factor is the square root of 252.

items.says: The research-wiki bullet may be lower priority than research results.
items.because: Documentation and onboarding detail is most valuable if space permits or the posting calls for it.

items.says: The candidate's share of the pipeline speedup is unclear.
items.because: Some of the improvement may have come from shared-cluster capability.

items.says: The candidate's author or contributor role in the JASA paper is unclear.
items.because: The reader should not have to infer the candidate's specific contribution.

items.says: The paper's current status should be unmistakable.
items.because: The reader should know whether it is a publication, submission, or work in progress.

items.says: The teaching bullet may be lower priority for industry research roles.
items.because: Research evidence may deserve the space instead.

items.says: The R-package result is crowded together with unrelated lab duties.
items.because: Several claims compete for attention and obscure the package's adoption evidence.

items.says: The 3,000-download count needs an accurate, defensible source.
items.because: The adoption claim should withstand scrutiny.

items.says: The evaluation setup needs to distinguish this HAR-RV result from the internship comparison.
items.because: The two results could otherwise be conflated.

items.says: The project should clarify whether its bullets share the same 30 indices and evaluation period.
items.because: Their scope is otherwise hard to compare.

items.says: The stated 33% improvement conflicts with the change from 0.20 to 0.15.
items.because: That change is a 25% reduction from the stated starting value.

items.says: The forecast-error result needs to be reconciled with the first bullet's 7% QLIKE result.
items.because: They risk looking like inconsistent versions of the same result.

items.says: The bullet repeats the first project's model and data scope.
items.because: Repetition dilutes the stronger result unless the outcome supplies meaningfully different evidence.

items.says: The rank and “top 2%” partly repeat the same placement.
items.because: “41st of 2,900” is more informative.

items.says: The competition context could be clearer.
items.because: Readers need enough context to understand the result.

items.says: The meaning of the 0.02 validation-to-leaderboard gap is unclear.
items.because: The metric behind the gap is not stated.

items.says: The leakage wording should not imply more was verified than the bullet establishes.
items.because: Reducing leakage does not necessarily show it was fully eliminated.

items.says: The feature-selection bullet overlaps with the competition bullet's feature-engineering story.
items.because: It should show a separate contribution rather than repeat the placement evidence.

items.says: Kafka's relevance is not explained by the experience entries.
items.because: It is less self-explanatory than Python or R in this context.

items.says: “Econometircs” is misspelled.
items.because: The intended methods term is “econometrics.”

items.says: The methods list lacks specifics behind the projects.
items.because: “High-dimensional statistics” is relevant but does not identify the particular methods used.
